record.notes: Published by the National Artificial Intelligence Centre on 5 September 2024 as the first version of Australia's AI safety standard. On 21 October 2025 the Centre published the Guidance for AI Adoption, which the DISR page describes as updated and simplified guidance for industry that evolves the standard. The Guidance calls itself the first update of the standard: it condensed the 10 guardrails into 6 essential practices, extended the guidance to AI developers as well as deployers, and integrated all of the standard's practices, with a crosswalk from each guardrail to the new practices.

Stored in this run from DISR and the National AI Centre: the standard's '10 guardrails' page (the guardrails in the summary) and the Guidance for AI Adoption implementation guidance PDF (October 2025), which calls itself the first update of the VAISS and says all VAISS practices are integrated into it. The earlier notes' statement that the standard was published together with the guardrails proposals paper is not in this record's stored files and was removed.

record.summary: Set 10 voluntary guardrails for organisations across the AI supply chain: an accountability process, risk management, data governance and protection of AI systems, testing and monitoring, meaningful human oversight, informing end-users about AI use and AI-generated content, processes to challenge AI outcomes, transparency across the supply chain, record-keeping, and stakeholder engagement focused on safety and fairness. It described what developers and deployers should do to use AI safely and used language aligned with international standards.

legal_force.quote: The standard consists of 10 voluntary guardrails that apply to all organisations throughout the AI supply chain.

summary.quote: 1. Establish, implement and publish an accountability process including governance, internal capability and a strategy for regulatory compliance.
3. Protect AI systems, and implement data governance measures to manage data quality and provenance.
5. Enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve meaningful human oversight across the life cycle.
6. Inform end-users regarding AI-enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI-generated content.
7. Establish processes for people impacted by AI systems to challenge use or outcomes.
9. Keep and maintain records to allow third parties to assess compliance with guardrails.
10. Engage your stakeholders and evaluate their needs and circumstances, with a focus on safety, diversity, inclusion and fairness.
They include transparency and accountability requirements across the supply chain. They also explain what developers and deployers of AI systems must do.
Some of the language in the standard is technical. We've chosen this language because it aligns with international standards.
